passages.title: The Name Card behind the Aquarium
passages.body: On Monday morning, Yui saw a small aquarium near the science room. Two classes had fish tanks, so she did not know which class used this one. The front card was missing. Yui looked at the feeding chart beside the tank. It said that Class 1-1 fed the fish on Monday and Wednesday. Then she found a name card behind the aquarium. It also said Class 1-1. Yui put the card back in front and spoke to her teacher about it. She used two clues before deciding, so she did not move the wrong aquarium.

passages.title: The Morning Worksheet in the Afternoon Tray
passages.body: Before first class, Kota went to collect the morning worksheets. He saw two trays on the teacher's desk. One said Morning and the other said Afternoon. Kota moved the worksheets to the Morning tray, and the class started with the correct pages.

A student named Miki Kato was in the chorus club. Hana took the case to the school office. Miki came there, and Hana and Miki looked at the place where Hana found it. The color was only one clue, but the initials and the room schedule made the answer much stronger.

passages.title: The Classroom Plant Watered Twice
passages.body: Mao's class had a small plant near the window. On Tuesday, Mao had the plant job before lunch. She touched the soil and saw that it was already wet. On the duty chart, no mark was beside Tuesday, so at first she thought no one had watered the plant. Then Riku came back and said he had watered it before homeroom but forgot the mark. Mao did not add more water. Riku put a check on the chart, and the class decided to mark the chart right after each job. The wet soil and Riku's words helped Mao avoid doing the same job twice.

passages.title: The Refill Station Used Mostly after PE
passages.body: The student council wanted to know when the new water refill station was busiest. At first, they counted users only during the ten-minute morning break and saw very few people. They almost decided that the station was not useful. Mei suggested checking other times. For three days, students counted users before school, after PE classes, at lunch, and after school. The largest numbers came just after PE, especially on warm afternoons. The council did not move the station. Instead, it added a second water container nearby during the two busiest periods and checked the line again. The waiting time became shorter. The wider time record changed their first conclusion and led to a small, useful change.

passages.title: The Cafeteria Tray Return Line beside the Exit
passages.body: After lunch, students returned trays along the wall beside the cafeteria exit. A teacher noticed that people leaving the room often crossed in front of students waiting with trays. The student council watched the area for two lunches. The crossing happened most often during the first five minutes after the bell, when both lines were long. Moving the tray table farther from the exit made the return line longer, so that idea was not good. Instead, the council changed the direction of the tray line and marked a separate walking lane to the door. On the next two days, students leaving the room did not need to cut through the return line. The new layout solved the crossing problem without adding another table, so the council kept it.

passages.title: The Used-Book Sale Sorted Only by Color
passages.body: For a used-book sale, volunteers arranged books on tables by cover color. The display looked bright, but visitors kept asking where to find novels, picture books, and science books. One volunteer wrote down the questions for thirty minutes. Most questions were about book type, not color. The group tried a second arrangement on one table. They made sections for stories, study books, picture books, and other books, then used small color cards inside each section. Visitors found books faster and asked fewer location questions. The volunteers changed the other tables before the next sale. They kept some color in the display, but they stopped using color as the main system because the test showed that buyers searched by content.

passages.title: The Classroom Microphone That Worked Only near the Front
passages.body: A class used a small microphone during presentations. Students near the front said the sound was clear, but several students in the back missed parts of each talk. The class first planned to buy a new microphone. Before spending money, they tested the room. One student read the same short paragraph while listeners sat in six different seats. The microphone itself was clear, but a speaker on the front wall made the back corner much quieter. The teacher moved the portable speaker to the center side of the room and repeated the test. All six listeners could hear the paragraph. The class kept the microphone and changed the speaker position instead. The seat-by-seat test showed that the problem was not the microphone they had first blamed.

passages.title: The Garden Mulch Test after Three Hot Days
passages.body: The gardening club wanted to know whether dry leaves on the soil could help the school garden keep water. They covered one small area with leaves and left another area open. After three very hot days, the covered soil was wetter. Some members wanted to put leaves everywhere immediately. Aya pointed out that all three test days had been unusually hot. The club continued the test for two more weeks and checked both areas after hot days and cooler days. The covered area usually kept more water, but the difference was much smaller in cool weather. The club used leaves around plants that dried quickly and continued watching the soil. The longer test supported the idea while also showing that weather changed how large the effect was.

passages.title: The Festival Map with Restrooms Hidden by the Legend
passages.body: The class created a map for the school festival. The map showed rooms, food areas, exits, and restrooms. On paper, every symbol was correct. During a trial, however, visitors needed extra time to find the restroom symbols because the map legend covered part of the lower floor plan. The designers asked six students to find the nearest restroom from three starting points. Four students first looked in the wrong direction. The group moved the legend to an empty corner and made the restroom symbols slightly larger. In the second test, all six students chose the correct route quickly. Nothing in the building had changed; only the way the information was shown had made the first map harder to use.

passages.title: The Volunteer Sign-Up Filled Mostly by One Class
passages.body: A community cleanup needed forty student volunteers. The first sign-up form was shared through one class's group message, and twenty-six students answered quickly. The organizers were happy until they checked the class names. Twenty-three of the twenty-six students were from the same class. Students in other grades had hardly seen the notice. The organizers did not treat the first list as a fair picture of school interest. They posted the same information on the school board, asked each homeroom teacher to mention it, and kept sign-up open for three more days. The final group included students from all three grades. The first form had found willing volunteers, but its delivery method had limited who had a chance to answer.

passages.title: The Lost-and-Found Photo Board without Dates
passages.body: The school office made a photo board for lost items. Students could see pictures of umbrellas, notebooks, towels, and bags. After two months, the board had more than fifty photos. Students often asked whether an item had been found yesterday or many weeks earlier because the photos had no dates. The office tried adding a found date and location under ten new photos. During the next week, students identified six items from those photos without asking for extra help. The staff then added dates to the older pictures that still had records and removed photos of items already returned. The board became smaller and easier to use. The problem had not been too few pictures; it was missing time information and old information that no longer needed to stay.

passages.title: The Bicycle Rack Entrance Blocked at Dismissal
passages.body: Most bicycles looked neatly parked during class time, so teachers thought the rack worked well. At dismissal, however, some students took bicycles out while other students came to unlock bicycles near the same narrow entrance. A safety group watched for fifteen minutes on three days. The largest crowd formed in the first seven minutes after the final bell. They tested moving five bicycle spaces away from the entrance and marking one side for people walking in and the other for bicycles moving out. The total number of spaces stayed the same because the five spaces were moved to the far end. During the next test, the entrance stayed open and students crossed less often. Looking only during quiet class time had hidden the problem.

passages.title: The Classroom Air Check Done beside One Open Window
passages.body: A science group measured classroom air during lunch. Their first sensor was placed beside an open window, and the reading looked very good. They planned to report that the whole room had enough fresh air. One student, Ken, asked whether the back corner would show the same result. The group moved the sensor to four places while keeping the windows in the same position. The back corner had a clearly different reading. They repeated the test on two more days and saw the same pattern. The class then changed how it opened the windows during lunch and checked the four places again. The readings became more similar. One measurement had been correct for the window area, but it could not describe the whole room.

passages.title: The Museum Guide Cards with Text Too Close Together
passages.body: The class created guide cards for a small local museum display. Each card had correct information, but several visitors read the first line and skipped the rest. The students first thought the visitors were not interested. Then they asked eight people to find one date and one person's name on a sample card. Most found the facts, but several said the lines were too close together and the important words were hard to see. The students increased the space between lines, made the key date and name slightly larger, and shortened one long sentence. In a second test, all eight people found the two facts faster. The content had been accurate from the start, but the layout had made accurate information harder to use.

passages.title: The Cooling-Room Survey Taken during One Cloudy Day
passages.body: A community center opened three cooling rooms for people to rest during hot weather. A student group wanted to compare the rooms and measured the temperature at 1:00 p.m. on one cloudy day. Room C was the coolest, so their first draft called it the best cooling room. Their adviser asked what would happen on a sunny afternoon. The group returned on four more days, including two clear days. Room C stayed cool on cloudy days, but strong afternoon sunlight entered its west windows on clear days. Room A, which had smaller north-facing windows, changed less. The students also asked visitors about noise and available seats. In their final report, they did not name one room as always best. They explained that Room C worked well in cloudy weather, while Room A was more stable on sunny afternoons and often had more open seats. A single correct measurement had not been enough for a general conclusion.

passages.title: The Closed Storefront Proposed as a Repair Workshop
passages.body: A shopping street had an empty storefront near the station. A youth group proposed using it as a weekend repair workshop where residents could bring small lamps, toys, and bicycles. At first, the idea seemed simple because the owner offered the space at a low trial rent. During planning, however, the group found several limits. The back room had only one narrow exit, so bicycle repair could not safely happen there. A music shop next door was worried about drilling noise during lessons. Some volunteers could repair electrical items, but no adult with that experience was available every weekend. The entrance also had a small step that made access difficult for some visitors. Instead of giving up, the group reduced the first trial to four Saturdays. Bicycle work moved to a covered space behind the building, drilling was limited to hours agreed with the music shop, and electrical repairs were accepted only on days when an experienced adult was present. The owner added a temporary ramp at the entrance. The group recorded visitor numbers, repair types, noise complaints, and unfinished jobs. After four weeks, demand was strongest for simple toy and bicycle repairs, while electrical requests were fewer but needed more supervision. The trial did not prove that every kind of repair workshop would work there. It showed which activities fit the space and what conditions were necessary for a safer long-term plan. The group also learned that clear limits made volunteers more confident about which repairs they should accept.

They planned to praise D as the most efficient building. A teacher noticed that the sports hall in Building D was used for weekend tournaments. The committee added Saturday and Sunday data for the same month. D's total rose sharply because lighting and air conditioning were used during several events. Building B then had the lowest use per day. The students also divided total electricity by the number of hours each building was open. After that calculation, the differences became smaller. passages.title: The Interview Quote Shortened on the School Website
passages.body: The school website published an interview with a student who organized a charity run. The page quoted her as saying, We should stop using paper signs. Some readers thought she wanted all paper information removed from future events. A journalism class listened to the original recording. Her full sentence was, We should stop using paper signs where a reusable board can do the same job, but we still need clear printed maps for visitors who ask for them. The shortened quote had removed an important limit and contrast. The class did not accuse the writer of inventing words because every word in the short quote was real. Instead, they explained that selecting only one part had changed the apparent meaning. The website restored the full sentence and added a note about the correction. The lesson was that accuracy requires attention to individual words and to the context that controls what those words mean.

passages.title: The Shared Kitchen Schedule and the Missing Cleaning Time
passages.body: A community center allowed local groups to reserve a shared kitchen in two-hour blocks. The schedule looked full but organized: one group finished at 12:00 and the next began at 12:00. After several weeks, the center received complaints about dirty counters and groups starting late. Staff first considered adding stricter penalties. Before doing that, they observed six bookings. Most groups used almost the full two hours for cooking and eating, so cleanup happened after the listed end time. The next group then entered while dishes or trash were still being removed. The schedule itself had no cleaning period. The center tested a new rule for one month. Each two-hour reservation included one hour and forty-five minutes for activity and fifteen minutes for required cleanup. A simple checklist in Japanese, English, and pictures showed which surfaces and equipment had to be checked. Groups that needed the full two hours for cooking could reserve the next block as well, but they could not use another group's time without booking it. During the trial, late starts dropped sharply and complaints about dirty counters fell. A few groups disliked losing fifteen minutes, but most said the clear ending routine made planning easier. The center kept the new schedule. passages.title: The Beach Bird Count Taken after a Loud Festival
passages.body: A biology club counted shorebirds on Monday morning and found far fewer birds than a guidebook suggested for that season. Music, lights, and cleanup vehicles had continued for hours. The students also checked another nearby beach that had not hosted an event, where counts remained stable. Their report kept the first low number but described the unusual conditions around it. passages.title: The Translated Safety Notice with Two Possible Meanings
passages.body: A sports center translated a notice about storing folding chairs after events. The English version said, Do not leave chairs near the door after closing. Some readers understood this to mean that chairs could stay near the door during the event, while others thought the rule applied whenever the door might be used. Staff checked the original Japanese rule. Its purpose was to keep the emergency route clear at all times, not only after the building closed. The translators rewrote the English notice as, Keep the doorway clear at all times. After each event, return folding chairs to the storage wall. They asked several students and visitors to explain the new wording in their own words. Everyone described the same basic rule. The first translation was grammatically possible, but its time phrase allowed two interpretations. Testing the meaning with readers was more useful than checking grammar alone. The revised notice also worked better when staff explained it aloud.

passages.title: The Community Seed Library and the Question of Return Rules
passages.body: A community center started a seed library where residents could take small packets of vegetable and flower seeds for free. The first rule asked users to return the same number of seeds after harvest. The idea sounded fair, but by autumn the staff noticed problems. New gardeners sometimes had no successful harvest, so they could not return seeds. Other users returned large amounts from plants that had crossed with different varieties, making the next year's results uncertain. A few popular seed types disappeared quickly because demand was much higher than the number returned. The center did not want to charge a fee because the project was meant to lower barriers for beginners. It organized a three-month review with gardeners and a local farmer. Under a new trial, returning seeds became optional, but anyone who returned them had to label the plant variety and growing location. The center also kept a small reserve of the most requested seeds instead of putting every packet out at once. Workshops taught users how to collect and dry seeds safely. During the next season, more beginners joined, and the reserve prevented the most popular varieties from disappearing early. Fewer seed packets were returned overall than under the old rule, but the returned seeds had clearer information and were more useful. The center judged the trial by access, seed quality, and supply stability rather than by the simple percentage returned. A rule that looked equal for everyone had not produced the most reliable system.

passages.title: The Local News Team Choosing between Speed and Verification
passages.body: A student news team reported on a burst water pipe near school. At 7:40 a.m., one student received a message saying that all roads around the school were closed. A second message said only the east gate road was blocked. The team wanted to post quickly because families were already traveling to school. Instead of choosing the more dramatic message, they checked several sources. The city road page listed one closure on East Street. A teacher standing near the west gate sent a photo showing cars still moving there. At 7:52, the school office confirmed that the east gate could not be used, but the west and south routes remained open. The team posted a short notice at 7:55 with the confirmed closure, alternative entrances, and a link to the city page. Ten minutes later, a social-media account repeated the claim that every road was closed. Some students asked why the school news had not posted that warning. The team explained which evidence it had checked and continued watching the official page. At 8:20, another street was temporarily closed for repair vehicles, so the team updated its notice and clearly marked the new time. The first post had taken fifteen minutes longer than simply repeating the earliest message, but it had avoided sending families away from routes that were still usable. The students later wrote a policy for urgent news: publish verified facts first, label uncertain reports as uncertain, keep timestamps visible, and correct changes openly. Speed mattered, but in a changing situation, an unsupported fast statement could create a second problem.

passages.title: The Community Bus Times, Clinic Reception, Road Work, and Return Train
passages.body:
Mika was helping her grandfather plan a visit to a community clinic in another town. He no longer drove long distances, so he wanted to travel by public transport. At first, Mika looked only at the clinic's reception time and chose the 8:45 community bus. According to the normal timetable, that bus reached the clinic stop at 9:15, so it seemed early enough. Then she noticed a road-work notice beside the timetable. From 9:00 a.m. to 11:00 a.m., buses using Hill Road could be delayed by about fifteen minutes. Both morning community buses used Hill Road. If the 8:45 bus had the full delay, it might reach the clinic stop at about 9:30. The clinic accepted patients until 10:00, so that was still possible, but Mika checked the rest of the plan instead of stopping there.

Her grandfather's visit usually took about fifty minutes after reception. The clinic was a ten-minute walk from Central Station. The return trains left at 10:42, 11:22, and 12:02. Mika realized that arriving around 9:30, completing reception, spending about fifty minutes at the clinic, and walking to the station could make the 10:42 train too uncertain. The 11:22 train was safer.

There was also an earlier 8:10 bus. It normally reached the clinic stop at 8:40, before the road-work period began. The clinic building opened at 8:50 and reception began at 9:00. Her grandfather did not mind waiting ten minutes outside and another ten minutes inside. Mika compared the two choices with him. passages.title: The Evacuation Center Map, Pet Area Rules, Bus Arrivals, and Rain Alert
passages.body:
During heavy rain, Haruto's family received an alert telling people near the river to prepare to move to an evacuation center. Haruto lived with his mother, his grandmother, and a small dog. His grandmother could walk slowly with a cane, but long distances were difficult for her. The family first considered Center A because it was only 600 meters from home. The map, however, showed a steep outdoor path for the final 150 meters. Center B was 1.4 kilometers away, but a city bus stopped directly in front of it.

Haruto then checked the pet rules. Center A allowed pets only in outdoor cages beside the parking area. Center B had a covered pet room in a separate part of the building. The family could not leave the dog at home during the river alert. A rain notice also said that stronger rain was expected after 6:30 p.m. The current time was 5:35.

The emergency bus list showed two buses from the neighborhood stop to Center B, at 5:55 and 6:25. The trip normally took twenty minutes, and the city asked residents who needed slower movement to use the earlier bus if possible. Haruto's mother asked, 'Should we walk to Center A immediately? It is closer.' Haruto compared the whole route, not only the distance. His grandmother would have to walk uphill outside near the end of the route, and the dog would stay in an outdoor cage while the rain became stronger.

They decided to take the 5:55 bus to Center B. The neighborhood stop was a five-minute walk from their house, so they could reach it with time to spare. The bus arrived at Center B at 6:15, before the stronger rain was expected. Volunteers helped Haruto's grandmother enter through a step-free door, and the dog went to the covered pet room.

The family did not choose Center B because it was farther or newer. They chose it because the bus reduced walking, the entrance worked for Haruto's grandmother, the covered pet room met the dog's needs, and the earlier bus arrived before the forecast became worse. The map, pet rules, bus times, and weather notice all mattered to the same decision.

passages.title: The Museum Rooms, Workshop Ages, Elevator Inspection, and Last Bus
passages.body:
Aki was planning a Saturday museum visit with her ten-year-old brother Ren and their grandmother. They wanted to attend one workshop and see the local-history room before taking the last convenient bus home. The museum schedule looked easy at first, but several conditions affected the plan.

The local-history room was on the third floor. The elevator would be closed for inspection from 1:00 to 2:00 p.m., although the stairs would remain open. Their grandmother could use stairs for one floor but not comfortably for three floors. The museum had two workshops that afternoon. A robot workshop ran from 12:20 to 1:00 and was for ages twelve and older. A picture-book workshop ran from 1:15 to 1:55 and was for ages eight to eleven. Ren was ten, so only the picture-book workshop matched his age. Aki was fifteen and could join the robot workshop, but the family wanted to stay together.

The local-history room opened all day. From the entrance, the elevator ride to the third floor took about five minutes including waiting. The picture-book room was on the first floor beside the entrance. The family arrived at 11:50. Aki first suggested seeing history after Ren's workshop, but the workshop ended at 1:55, five minutes before the elevator inspection ended. They could wait until 2:00 before going upstairs, but that left a narrow window before the bus. That was possible, but the last convenient bus left the museum stop at 2:35, and they wanted at least twenty minutes in the history room. Five minutes to go up after 2:00, twenty minutes in the room, and about five minutes to return would bring them close to 2:30. One slow elevator wait could make the bus uncertain.

They chose a safer order. From 11:55 to 12:35, they visited the local-history room while the elevator was operating. They returned to the first floor well before 1:00 and ate lunch in the rest area. Ren joined the picture-book workshop from 1:15 to 1:55 while Aki and their grandmother waited nearby. Afterward, they looked at the museum shop and left for the 2:35 bus.

The age rule decided which workshop Ren could attend, but the elevator notice and bus time decided the order of the whole visit. By moving the third-floor room earlier, the family avoided making their return depend on a very narrow time window.

passages.title: The Summer Event Schedule, Heat Alert, Shade Map, Water Stations, and Shuttle Times
passages.body:
Nao's class planned to visit a summer science event in a large riverside park. The event had three activities the class wanted to compare: a solar-car demonstration, a river-insect talk, and a short outdoor experiment. Two days before the visit, the city issued a heat notice predicting the highest risk between 12:30 and 3:00 p.m. The teachers decided that students could still attend, but outdoor time during that period should be limited and every group needed a clear water and shade plan.

Nao studied the event map. The solar-car demonstration was in Open Field A at 12:40 and 2:10. The field had no permanent shade. The river-insect talk was in a covered pavilion at 1:20 and 2:40. The outdoor experiment was beside Garden C at 11:50 and 1:50. Garden C had a shaded rest area fifty meters away. Water stations were beside the entrance, the pavilion, and Garden C, but there was no water station in Open Field A.

The class shuttle arrived at 11:25. Return shuttles left at 2:20 and 3:20. Nao's group first wanted the 12:40 solar-car demonstration because it fit neatly between the experiment and the talk. However, that would place them in an unshaded field shortly after the high-risk period began. The later 2:10 demonstration was also during the high-risk period and ended too close to the 2:20 shuttle. Choosing it would almost require the 3:20 return.

The group changed its priorities. They attended the 11:50 outdoor experiment before the highest-risk period, rested and drank water at Garden C, then moved to the covered pavilion for the 1:20 river-insect talk. They skipped the solar-car demonstration and used the shaded pavilion area for a teacher-led explanation of the display information instead. After another water stop, they took the 2:20 shuttle home.

Some students were disappointed because the solar cars were exciting. Nao explained that the plan was not based on heat alone. The time of the warning, the lack of shade and water at Field A, the activity times, and the shuttle schedule all made the two solar-car options less suitable for this class visit. The group still completed two science activities and returned before the hottest part of the afternoon was over.

For the optional writing task, students were asked to give one 20-30 word recommendation for another class visiting the event on a hot day and include a reason connected to the schedule or map.
passages.fullTranslation:
ナオのクラスは大きな川沿い公園で開かれる夏の科学イベントへ行く計画を立てました。比べたい活動は、ソーラーカー実演、川の昆虫についての話、短い屋外実験の三つです。訪問2日前、市は午後12時30分から3時まで危険度が最も高いという暑さのお知らせを出しました。先生たちは参加自体は可能と判断しましたが、その時間帯の屋外活動を短くし、各グループが水分と日陰の計画を持つことにしました。

ナオは地図を調べました。ソーラーカー実演はOpen Field Aで12時40分と2時10分に行われます。Field Aには常設の日陰がありません。川の昆虫の話は屋根付きパビリオンで1時20分と2時40分。屋外実験はGarden Cの横で11時50分と1時50分です。Garden Cには50メートル先に日陰の休憩場所があります。給水場所は入口、パビリオン、Garden Cのそばにありますが、Open Field Aにはありません。

クラスのシャトルは11時25分に到着しました。帰りのシャトルは2時20分と3時20分です。ナオのグループは最初、実験と昆虫の話の間にきれいに入る12時40分のソーラーカー実演を希望しました。しかし危険度の高い時間が始まった直後に日陰のない場所へ行くことになります。2時10分の回も危険時間帯で、終了が2時20分のシャトルに近すぎます。それを選ぶと、ほぼ3時20分便を使う必要があります。

そこで優先順位を変えました。最も危険な時間帯より前の11時50分に屋外実験へ参加し、Garden Cで休んで水を飲み、その後屋根付きパビリオンで1時20分の昆虫の話を聞きました。ソーラーカー実演は見送って、日陰のパビリオン周辺で先生から展示情報について説明を受けました。もう一度水を飲み、2時20分のシャトルで帰りました。

ソーラーカーを楽しみにしていた生徒もいました。ナオは、判断が単に「暑いから」ではないと説明しました。警報の時間、Field Aに日陰と給水場所がないこと、活動時刻、シャトル時刻を合わせると、二つのソーラーカー回は今回のクラス訪問には適しにくかったのです。それでも二つの科学活動を終え、午後の最も暑い時間帯が終わる前に帰ることができました。

別枠の英作文では、暑い日にこのイベントを訪れる別のクラスへのおすすめを20〜30語で一つ書き、予定表または地図に関係する理由を含めるよう求めます。
